Chapter 7: The Multiplier Effect in Closed and Open Economies

kapitaali.com
April 14, 2026

Algebraic Derivation and Extensions

“The multiplier is not one number but a family of numbers, indexed by the model’s assumptions about money markets, expectations, and openness.”

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 8 (Keynesian cross and all multiplier types); Ch. 26 (open economy, import leakages); Ch. 28 (fiscal policy in practice, ARRA) [P:Ch.8, P:Ch.26, P:Ch.28]

7.1 The Keynesian Cross as a Fixed-Point Problem¶

Principles Chapter 8 introduced the Keynesian cross by means of a diagram: draw the 45-degree line and the expenditure function; equilibrium is their intersection. Here we reformulate this as a fixed-point problem in YYY, which yields both the existence and uniqueness of equilibrium and the precise multiplier formula from a single piece of mathematics.

The goods-market equilibrium condition is:

Y=E(Y;G,T,Iˉ),E(Y)=a+b(Y−T)+Iˉ+G,Y = \mathcal{E}(Y; G, T, \bar{I}), \quad \mathcal{E}(Y) = a + b(Y-T) + \bar{I} + G,Y=E(Y;G,T,Iˉ),E(Y)=a+b(Y−T)+Iˉ+G,
(1)

where E(Y)\mathcal{E}(Y)E(Y) is aggregate planned expenditure as a function of income YYY (treating GGG, TTT, and Iˉ\bar{I}Iˉ as parameters). Define the excess demand function:

ϕ(Y)≡E(Y)−Y=a+b(Y−T)+Iˉ+G−Y=Aˉ−(1−b)Y,\phi(Y) \equiv \mathcal{E}(Y) - Y = a + b(Y-T) + \bar{I} + G - Y = \bar{A} - (1-b)Y,ϕ(Y)≡E(Y)−Y=a+b(Y−T)+Iˉ+G−Y=Aˉ−(1−b)Y,
(2)

where Aˉ=a−bT+Iˉ+G\bar{A} = a - bT + \bar{I} + GAˉ=a−bT+Iˉ+G is autonomous expenditure. Equilibrium requires ϕ(Y∗)=0\phi(Y^*) = 0ϕ(Y∗)=0, i.e., Aˉ=(1−b)Y∗\bar{A} = (1-b)Y^*Aˉ=(1−b)Y∗, giving Y∗=Aˉ/(1−b)=κGAˉY^* = \bar{A}/(1-b) = \kappa_G\bar{A}Y∗=Aˉ/(1−b)=κG​Aˉ.

The contraction mapping argument: Consider the iteration Yn+1=E(Yn)Y_{n+1} = \mathcal{E}(Y_n)Yn+1​=E(Yn​). This defines a sequence (Y0,Y1,Y2,…)(Y_0, Y_1, Y_2, \ldots)(Y0​,Y1​,Y2​,…) starting from any Y0Y_0Y0​.

Definition 7.1 (Contraction Mapping). A function f:R→Rf: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}f:R→R is a contraction on R\mathbb{R}R if there exists λ∈[0,1)\lambda \in [0,1)λ∈[0,1) such that ∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤λ∣x−y∣|f(x) - f(y)| \leq \lambda|x - y|∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤λ∣x−y∣ for all x,yx, yx,y.

Theorem 7.1 (Banach Fixed-Point Theorem, Scalar Version). If fff is a contraction on a complete metric space, then fff has a unique fixed point x∗x^*x∗ and the iteration xn+1=f(xn)x_{n+1} = f(x_n)xn+1​=f(xn​) converges to x∗x^*x∗ from any starting point x0x_0x0​.

Application to the Keynesian cross. The expenditure function E(Y)=Aˉ+bY\mathcal{E}(Y) = \bar{A} + bYE(Y)=Aˉ+bY is a contraction with Lipschitz constant b=E′(Y)∈(0,1)b = \mathcal{E}'(Y) \in (0,1)b=E′(Y)∈(0,1) — precisely the MPC. Since b<1b < 1b<1, the iteration Yn+1=E(Yn)=Aˉ+bYnY_{n+1} = \mathcal{E}(Y_n) = \bar{A} + bY_nYn+1​=E(Yn​)=Aˉ+bYn​ converges to the unique fixed point Y∗=Aˉ/(1−b)Y^* = \bar{A}/(1-b)Y∗=Aˉ/(1−b) from any starting income Y0Y_0Y0​.

The speed of convergence: ∣Yn−Y∗∣=bn∣Y0−Y∗∣|Y_n - Y^*| = b^n|Y_0 - Y^*|∣Yn​−Y∗∣=bn∣Y0​−Y∗∣. Each “round” of the multiplier process — firms produce, workers earn income, households spend fraction bbb, firms produce again — shrinks the gap from equilibrium by factor bbb. After nnn rounds, the remaining gap is bnb^nbn of the original.

Definition 7.2 (The Keynesian Multiplier). The Keynesian (government spending) multiplier is:

κG=∂Y∗∂G=11−b.\kappa_G = \frac{\partial Y^*}{\partial G} = \frac{1}{1-b}.κG​=∂G∂Y∗​=1−b1​.
(3)

It equals the sum of the geometric series ∑n=0∞bn=1/(1−b)\sum_{n=0}^\infty b^n = 1/(1-b)∑n=0∞​bn=1/(1−b): the first-round effect (1 dollar of spending), plus the second-round effect (bbb dollars of induced consumption), plus the third round (b2b^2b2), and so on.

7.2 All Six Multipliers: Complete Algebraic Derivation¶

The Keynesian cross with proportional income tax rate ttt (so tax revenue is T=tY+T0T = tY + T_0T=tY+T0​ with lump-sum component T0T_0T0​) and transfer payments TRTRTR:

Y=a+b(Y−tY−T0+TR)+Iˉ+G.Y = a + b(Y - tY - T_0 + TR) + \bar{I} + G.Y=a+b(Y−tY−T0​+TR)+Iˉ+G.
(4)

Collecting terms:

Y[1−b(1−t)]=a−bT0+bTR+Iˉ+G⏟Aˉeff.Y[1 - b(1-t)] = \underbrace{a - bT_0 + bTR + \bar{I} + G}_{\bar{A}^{eff}}.Y[1−b(1−t)]=Aˉeffa−bT0​+bTR+Iˉ+G​​.
(5)

Definition 7.3 (Effective Multiplier Denominator). The expression 1−b(1−t)1 - b(1-t)1−b(1−t) is the effective leakage rate: the fraction of each dollar of income that “leaks out” of the spending stream through saving (1−b)(1-b)(1−b) and taxes on marginal income (bt)(bt)(bt).

Y∗=Aˉeff1−b(1−t)≡κeffAˉeff.Y^* = \frac{\bar{A}^{eff}}{1 - b(1-t)} \equiv \kappa^{eff}\bar{A}^{eff}.Y∗=1−b(1−t)Aˉeff​≡κeffAˉeff.
(6)

Multiplier 1 — Government spending multiplier:

μG=∂Y∗∂G=11−b(1−t).\mu_G = \frac{\partial Y^*}{\partial G} = \frac{1}{1-b(1-t)}.μG​=∂G∂Y∗​=1−b(1−t)1​.
(7)

Multiplier 2 — Lump-sum tax multiplier:

μT0=∂Y∗∂T0=−b1−b(1−t).\mu_{T_0} = \frac{\partial Y^*}{\partial T_0} = \frac{-b}{1-b(1-t)}.μT0​​=∂T0​∂Y∗​=1−b(1−t)−b​.
(8)

Multiplier 3 — Proportional tax rate multiplier:

μt=∂Y∗∂t=−bY∗[1−b(1−t)]2⋅[1−b(1−t)]−∂Y∗∂t⋅0=−bY∗1−b(1−t)<0.\mu_t = \frac{\partial Y^*}{\partial t} = \frac{-bY^*}{[1-b(1-t)]^2} \cdot [1-b(1-t)] - \frac{\partial Y^*}{\partial t}\cdot0 = \frac{-bY^*}{1-b(1-t)} < 0.μt​=∂t∂Y∗​=[1−b(1−t)]2−bY∗​⋅[1−b(1−t)]−∂t∂Y∗​⋅0=1−b(1−t)−bY∗​<0.
(9)

A higher tax rate reduces the effective multiplier and, at any given income level, reduces equilibrium income. The effect depends on Y∗Y^*Y∗ itself (because the tax base is income), making this a nonlinear comparative static.

Multiplier 4 — Transfer payment multiplier:

μTR=∂Y∗∂TR=b1−b(1−t)=b⋅μG.\mu_{TR} = \frac{\partial Y^*}{\partial TR} = \frac{b}{1-b(1-t)} = b\cdot\mu_G.μTR​=∂TR∂Y∗​=1−b(1−t)b​=b⋅μG​.
(10)

Transfers are less stimulative than direct spending: a dollar of transfers raises disposable income by one dollar, of which only fraction bbb is spent. A dollar of government purchases creates a full dollar of first-round demand.

Multiplier 5 — The Balanced-Budget Multiplier (Haavelmo’s theorem):

Suppose ΔG=ΔT0=ΔB\Delta G = \Delta T_0 = \Delta BΔG=ΔT0​=ΔB (spending and lump-sum taxes increase equally):

ΔY∗=μGΔB+μT0ΔB=11−b(1−t)ΔB−b1−b(1−t)ΔB=1−b1−b(1−t)ΔB.\Delta Y^* = \mu_G\Delta B + \mu_{T_0}\Delta B = \frac{1}{1-b(1-t)}\Delta B - \frac{b}{1-b(1-t)}\Delta B = \frac{1-b}{1-b(1-t)}\Delta B.ΔY∗=μG​ΔB+μT0​​ΔB=1−b(1−t)1​ΔB−1−b(1−t)b​ΔB=1−b(1−t)1−b​ΔB.
(11)

Theorem 7.2 (Haavelmo’s Theorem, General Form). When government spending and lump-sum taxes both increase by ΔB\Delta BΔB, output rises by:

ΔY∗=1−b1−b(1−t)ΔB.\Delta Y^* = \frac{1-b}{1-b(1-t)}\Delta B.ΔY∗=1−b(1−t)1−b​ΔB.
(12)

With t=0t = 0t=0 (lump-sum taxes only), this reduces to ΔY∗=1−b1−bΔB=ΔB\Delta Y^* = \frac{1-b}{1-b}\Delta B = \Delta BΔY∗=1−b1−b​ΔB=ΔB: the balanced budget multiplier is exactly 1.

Proof (general case, t=0t = 0t=0):

ΔY∗=κGΔB+μT0ΔB=11−bΔB−b1−bΔB=1−b1−bΔB=ΔB.\Delta Y^* = \kappa_G\Delta B + \mu_{T_0}\Delta B = \frac{1}{1-b}\Delta B - \frac{b}{1-b}\Delta B = \frac{1-b}{1-b}\Delta B = \Delta B.ΔY∗=κG​ΔB+μT0​​ΔB=1−b1​ΔB−1−bb​ΔB=1−b1−b​ΔB=ΔB. □\square□

The economic intuition: government spends every dollar of tax revenue, while households would have saved fraction (1−b)(1-b)(1−b). The government therefore contributes more to aggregate demand per dollar taxed than households would have. The net gain equals exactly the saved fraction: ΔY∗=1−∣μT0∣=1−b/(1−b)⋅(1−b)=1\Delta Y^* = 1 - |\mu_{T_0}| = 1 - b/(1-b) \cdot (1-b) = 1ΔY∗=1−∣μT0​​∣=1−b/(1−b)⋅(1−b)=1... but wait — with t=0t = 0t=0, μG=1/(1−b)\mu_G = 1/(1-b)μG​=1/(1−b) and ∣μT0∣=b/(1−b)|\mu_{T_0}| = b/(1-b)∣μT0​​∣=b/(1−b), so ΔY∗=[1/(1−b)−b/(1−b)]ΔB=ΔB\Delta Y^* = [1/(1-b) - b/(1-b)]\Delta B = \Delta BΔY∗=[1/(1−b)−b/(1−b)]ΔB=ΔB. The balanced budget multiplier is 1, independent of bbb. A remarkable result.

Multiplier 6 — Investment multiplier:

μIˉ=∂Y∗∂Iˉ=11−b(1−t)=μG.\mu_{\bar{I}} = \frac{\partial Y^*}{\partial\bar{I}} = \frac{1}{1-b(1-t)} = \mu_G.μIˉ​=∂Iˉ∂Y∗​=1−b(1−t)1​=μG​.
(13)

An autonomous increase in investment — an animal spirits boom [P:Ch.15.4] — has the same multiplied effect on output as an equivalent increase in government spending.

7.3 The Open-Economy Multiplier and Import Leakages¶

In an open economy, some of each round of induced spending falls on imports rather than domestically produced goods [P:Ch.26.5]. This import leakage reduces the multiplier.

With import function IM=m0+mYYIM = m_0 + m_Y YIM=m0​+mY​Y (where mY>0m_Y > 0mY​>0 is the marginal propensity to import), the open-economy equilibrium:

Y=a+b(Y−T)+Iˉ+G+X−m0−mYY,Y = a + b(Y-T) + \bar{I} + G + X - m_0 - m_Y Y,Y=a+b(Y−T)+Iˉ+G+X−m0​−mY​Y,
(14)

where XXX is autonomous exports. Collecting:

Y[1−b(1−t)+mY]=Aˉopen.Y[1 - b(1-t) + m_Y] = \bar{A}^{open}.Y[1−b(1−t)+mY​]=Aˉopen.
(15)

Multiplier 7 — Open-economy government spending multiplier:

μGopen=11−b(1−t)+mY<μGclosed.\mu_G^{open} = \frac{1}{1-b(1-t)+m_Y} < \mu_G^{closed}.μGopen​=1−b(1−t)+mY​1​<μGclosed​.
(16)

The import leakage mYm_YmY​ in the denominator reduces the multiplier: income generated by fiscal expansion partly flows abroad as import demand, weakening the domestic income circuit.

Definition 7.4 (Propensity to Spend on Domestic Output). Define b~=b(1−t)−mY\tilde{b} = b(1-t) - m_Yb~=b(1−t)−mY​ as the net marginal propensity to spend on domestic output — the fraction of each additional dollar of income that re-enters the domestic spending stream. The open-economy multiplier is simply:

μGopen=11−b~.\mu_G^{open} = \frac{1}{1-\tilde{b}}.μGopen​=1−b~1​.
(17)

This unifies all six multipliers: they all take the form 1/(1−b~)1/(1-\tilde{b})1/(1−b~) where b~\tilde{b}b~ accounts for whatever leakages are present (saving, taxes, imports, and in the IS–LM context, the interest rate feedback via crowding out).

Table of leakages and their effects on multipliers:

Leakage sourceReduces denominator byEffect on μG\mu_GμG​
Saving (MPS)+(1−b)+(1-b)+(1−b)Reduces multiplier
Proportional tax+bt+bt+btReduces multiplier
Import propensity+mY+m_Y+mY​Reduces multiplier

7.4 The Propensity to Spend: Sensitivity Analysis¶

The multiplier κ=1/(1−b)\kappa = 1/(1-b)κ=1/(1−b) is extremely sensitive to the MPC bbb near b=1b = 1b=1:

dκdb=1(1−b)2→∞ as b→1.\frac{d\kappa}{db} = \frac{1}{(1-b)^2} \to \infty \text{ as } b\to 1.dbdκ​=(1−b)21​→∞ as b→1.
(18)

At b=0.75b = 0.75b=0.75: κ=4\kappa = 4κ=4. At b=0.80b = 0.80b=0.80: κ=5\kappa = 5κ=5. At b=0.90b = 0.90b=0.90: κ=10\kappa = 10κ=10. At b=0.95b = 0.95b=0.95: κ=20\kappa = 20κ=20.

This sensitivity has important implications for policy analysis. The MPC is not a structural constant — it varies across:

  1. Households by income and wealth: liquidity-constrained households have b≈1b \approx 1b≈1 (they spend every dollar of income); wealthy households have b≈0.3b \approx 0.3b≈0.3–0.5 (Kaplan et al., 2018, HANK model [P:Ch.25.3]).

  2. Type of fiscal transfer: lump-sum cash transfers have high MPCs for constrained recipients; corporate tax cuts have low MPCs if they flow to wealthy shareholders.

  3. Expectations about permanence: permanent income changes have higher MPCs than transitory ones (PIH, [P:Ch.11.2]).

The elasticity of the multiplier with respect to the MPC:

εκ,b=dκdb⋅bκ=b(1−b)2⋅1−b1=b1−b.\varepsilon_{\kappa,b} = \frac{d\kappa}{db}\cdot\frac{b}{\kappa} = \frac{b}{(1-b)^2}\cdot\frac{1-b}{1} = \frac{b}{1-b}.εκ,b​=dbdκ​⋅κb​=(1−b)2b​⋅11−b​=1−bb​.
(19)

At b=0.75b = 0.75b=0.75: ε=3\varepsilon = 3ε=3. A 1% increase in the MPC raises the multiplier by 3%. This high elasticity means that the policy effectiveness of fiscal stimulus depends critically on who receives it — and whether recipients are constrained.

7.5 The Geometric Series Derivation: Round-by-Round Accounting¶

The multiplier formula κG=1/(1−b)=∑n=0∞bn\kappa_G = 1/(1-b) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty b^nκG​=1/(1−b)=∑n=0∞​bn connects to a concrete narrative about how spending circulates through the economy.

Round 0: Government increases spending by ΔG=1\Delta G = 1ΔG=1. Output rises by 1.

Round 1: The dollar of output becomes income for workers and owners. They spend fraction bbb: induced consumption ΔC1=b\Delta C_1 = bΔC1​=b. Output rises by an additional bbb.

Round 2: The additional bbb of output becomes income. Fraction bbb is spent: ΔC2=b2\Delta C_2 = b^2ΔC2​=b2. Output rises by b2b^2b2.

Round nnn: ΔCn=bn\Delta C_n = b^nΔCn​=bn.

Total: ∑n=0∞bn=1/(1−b)=κG\sum_{n=0}^\infty b^n = 1/(1-b) = \kappa_G∑n=0∞​bn=1/(1−b)=κG​.

The sum converges because b<1b < 1b<1: each round the increment is smaller by factor bbb, and the infinite sum is finite. If b=1b = 1b=1 (no saving), the sum diverges — a $1\$1$1 spending becomes infinite output. If b=0b = 0b=0 (all saving), the sum is 1 — the multiplier equals one because no induced spending occurs.

In APL, the round-by-round accumulation is a natural scan operation:

⎕IO←0 ⋄ ⎕ML←1

b ← 0.75
n_rounds ← 20

⍝ Round-by-round increments: b^0, b^1, ..., b^(n-1)
increments ← b * ⍳ n_rounds      ⍝ geometric sequence

⍝ Cumulative sum = partial sum of multiplier series
cumulative ← +\ increments        ⍝ scan: running total

⍝ Theoretical limit
kappa_G ← ÷ 1 - b                 ⍝ = 4.0

⍝ Convergence check: how many rounds to reach 99% of limit?
pct_of_limit ← cumulative ÷ kappa_G
n_99pct ← +/ pct_of_limit < 0.99  ⍝ count rounds below 99%
'Rounds to reach 99% limit: ' n_99pct    ⍝ ≈ 14 rounds for b=0.75
Loading...

7.6 Worked Example: The 2009 ARRA Multiplier¶

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 28.2 (ARRA empirical evidence) [P:Ch.28.2]

The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (2009) provided $787\$787$787 billion in stimulus over 10 years. A naive Keynesian cross calculation with b=0.75b = 0.75b=0.75 and no leakages gives κG=4\kappa_G = 4κG​=4 — the stimulus should have raised GDP by over $3\$3$3 trillion. The actual impact was far smaller. Why?

Calibrating with leakages:

Let b=0.75b = 0.75b=0.75, t=0.28t = 0.28t=0.28 (effective marginal federal plus state income tax rate), mY=0.12m_Y = 0.12mY​=0.12 (import propensity), br=1.5b_r = 1.5br​=1.5 (investment-interest sensitivity), h=4h = 4h=4 (interest semi-elasticity), k=0.5k = 0.5k=0.5 (income elasticity of money demand).

IS–LM multiplier (closed):

μGclosed=hh(1−b)+brk=44(0.25)+1.5×0.5=41+0.75=41.75=2.29.\mu_G^{closed} = \frac{h}{h(1-b)+b_r k} = \frac{4}{4(0.25)+1.5\times0.5} = \frac{4}{1+0.75} = \frac{4}{1.75} = 2.29.μGclosed​=h(1−b)+br​kh​=4(0.25)+1.5×0.54​=1+0.754​=1.754​=2.29.
(20)

Adding proportional tax:

μGtax=11−b(1−t)=11−0.75×0.72=10.46=2.17.\mu_G^{tax} = \frac{1}{1-b(1-t)} = \frac{1}{1-0.75\times0.72} = \frac{1}{0.46} = 2.17.μGtax​=1−b(1−t)1​=1−0.75×0.721​=0.461​=2.17.
(21)

Adding imports (IS–LM with open economy):

μGopen, IS−LM=hh(1−b(1−t)+mY)+brk(1−b(1−t)+mY)/(1).\mu_G^{open,\,IS-LM} = \frac{h}{h(1-b(1-t)+m_Y)+b_r k(1-b(1-t)+m_Y)/(1)}.μGopen,IS−LM​=h(1−b(1−t)+mY​)+br​k(1−b(1−t)+mY​)/(1)h​.
(22)

With the combined denominator (1−b(1−t)+mY)=0.46+0.12=0.58(1-b(1-t)+m_Y) = 0.46 + 0.12 = 0.58(1−b(1−t)+mY​)=0.46+0.12=0.58 replacing (1−b)(1-b)(1−b):

μGfull=hh⋅0.58+br⋅k=42.32+0.75=43.07=1.30.\mu_G^{full} = \frac{h}{h\cdot0.58 + b_r\cdot k} = \frac{4}{2.32+0.75} = \frac{4}{3.07} = 1.30.μGfull​=h⋅0.58+br​⋅kh​=2.32+0.754​=3.074​=1.30.
(23)

At the ELB (estimated): With h→∞h\to\inftyh→∞ (zero crowding out), the ELB multiplier:

μGELB=11−b(1−t)+mY=10.58=1.72.\mu_G^{ELB} = \frac{1}{1-b(1-t)+m_Y} = \frac{1}{0.58} = 1.72.μGELB​=1−b(1−t)+mY​1​=0.581​=1.72.
(24)

This is consistent with the Romer–Bernstein (2009) projection of 1.57 and the Nakamura–Steinsson (2014) cross-state estimate of approximately 1.5–2.0 [P:Ch.28.2].

The lesson: the naive multiplier of 4 reflects a closed economy at the liquidity trap with no taxes or imports. Each realistic modification reduces it. Fiscal policy remains stimulative, but the magnitude depends critically on the model calibration.

⎕IO←0 ⋄ ⎕ML←1

⍝ 1. Parameters
b ← 0.75   ⋄ t ← 0.28    ⋄ m_Y ← 0.12  
b_r ← 1.5  ⋄ h ← 4       ⋄ k ← 0.5

⍝ 2. Progressive multiplier calculations
⍝ Note: we use parentheses to ensure denominators are fully calculated before division
mu_naive ← ÷ 1 - b                                 ⍝ Simple: 4.0
mu_tax   ← ÷ 1 - b × 1 - t                         ⍝ + Tax leakage: ~2.17
mu_open  ← ÷ m_Y + 1 - b × 1 - t                   ⍝ + Import leakage: ~1.72

⍝ IS-LM Crowding out (Closed)
⍝ Formula: h / (h(1-b(1-t)) + br*k)
denom_closed ← (b_r × k) + h × 1 - b × 1 - t
mu_islm  ← h ÷ denom_closed

⍝ Full leakage (Open + Crowding Out)
⍝ Formula: h / (h(1-b(1-t) + m_y) + br*k)
denom_full ← (b_r × k) + h × m_Y + 1 - b × 1 - t
mu_full ← h ÷ denom_full

⍝ 3. Display as a table
labels ← 'Naive' 'Tax' 'Open(ELB)' 'ISLM(closed)' 'Full'
values ← mu_naive mu_tax mu_open mu_islm mu_full

Exercise 7.2 (Python — MPC Sensitivity)¶

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

b_vals = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 500)
# Three multipliers as functions of b (t=0.25, m_Y=0.10)
t, m_Y = 0.25, 0.10
mu_closed = 1 / (1-b_vals)
mu_tax    = 1 / (1-b_vals*(1-t))
mu_open   = 1 / (1-b_vals*(1-t)+m_Y)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(b_vals, mu_closed, label='Closed, no tax')
ax.plot(b_vals, mu_tax,    label='Closed, with tax t=0.25')
ax.plot(b_vals, mu_open,   label='Open, t=0.25, m_Y=0.10')
ax.axvline(0.75, linestyle='--', color='gray', alpha=0.5, label='b=0.75')
ax.set_ylim(0, 15); ax.set_xlabel('MPC (b)'); ax.set_ylabel('Multiplier')
ax.legend(); plt.title('Keynesian Multiplier vs. MPC'); plt.show()

Exercise 7.3 (Julia — Round-by-Round Convergence)¶

b = 0.80; n = 30
increments = b .^ (0:n-1)
cumulative = cumsum(increments)
limit = 1/(1-b)

println("Rounds to 90% of limit: ", findfirst(cumulative ./ limit .>= 0.90))
println("Rounds to 99% of limit: ", findfirst(cumulative ./ limit .>= 0.99))
println("Rounds to 99.9%:        ", findfirst(cumulative ./ limit .>= 0.999))
# Verify: at b=0.8, convergence is slower than b=0.75

Exercise 7.4 (R — ARRA Calibration Sweep)¶

# Sweep over (b, t, m_Y) to find range of plausible ARRA multipliers
b_vals <- seq(0.5, 0.9, 0.05)
t_vals <- seq(0.20, 0.35, 0.05)
m_Y    <- 0.12

# ELB multiplier: no crowding out
mu_grid <- outer(b_vals, t_vals, function(b, t) 1/(1-b*(1-t)+m_Y))
rownames(mu_grid) <- paste0("b=", b_vals)
colnames(mu_grid) <- paste0("t=", t_vals)
round(mu_grid, 2)

7.8 Chapter Summary¶

Key results:

  • The Keynesian cross equilibrium is a fixed point of the expenditure function E(Y)\mathcal{E}(Y)E(Y); the contraction mapping theorem guarantees existence and uniqueness when b<1b < 1b<1.

  • The six multipliers for the closed economy with proportional taxes:

    • Spending: μG=1/[1−b(1−t)]\mu_G = 1/[1-b(1-t)]μG​=1/[1−b(1−t)]

    • Lump-sum tax: μT0=−b/[1−b(1−t)]\mu_{T_0} = -b/[1-b(1-t)]μT0​​=−b/[1−b(1−t)]

    • Transfer: μTR=b/[1−b(1−t)]\mu_{TR} = b/[1-b(1-t)]μTR​=b/[1−b(1−t)]

    • Balanced budget: μBB=(1−b)/[1−b(1−t)]≤1\mu_{BB} = (1-b)/[1-b(1-t)] \leq 1μBB​=(1−b)/[1−b(1−t)]≤1

    • Investment: μIˉ=μG\mu_{\bar{I}} = \mu_GμIˉ​=μG​

    • Open economy: μGopen=1/[1−b(1−t)+mY]\mu_G^{open} = 1/[1-b(1-t)+m_Y]μGopen​=1/[1−b(1−t)+mY​]

  • Haavelmo’s theorem: with lump-sum taxes and t=0t = 0t=0, the balanced-budget multiplier is exactly 1, independent of the MPC.

  • Every multiplier takes the form 1/(1−b~)1/(1-\tilde{b})1/(1−b~) where b~\tilde{b}b~ is the net marginal propensity to spend on domestic output, unifying all cases.

  • In APL: the round-by-round accumulation is +\ b * ⍳ n_rounds (scan of geometric sequence); the full multiplier table is generated via ∘.f outer product over parameter grids.

Connections forward: Chapter 9 derives the ELB multiplier — the analogous formula for the dynamic NK model at the zero lower bound, where crowding out is absent and forward-looking inflation expectations amplify the fiscal effect beyond 1/(1−b~)1/(1-\tilde{b})1/(1−b~).
